summary: Thousands of protesters in Egypt staged unprecedented anti-government demonstrations demanding President Hosni Mubarak's resignation, resulting in three deaths and at least 49 injuries.
Egyptian security forces crack down on anti-government protesters demanding the ouster of President Hosni Mubarak, using water cannons and tear gas and arresting at least 90 people in Cairo.
Egyptian demonstrators protest against President Hosni Mubarak's rule, including tearing a portrait of him in Alexandria.
Protesters in Egypt demonstrate against growing inequality, nepotism, and police brutality, driven largely by young people and the educated middle class.

The banned Muslim Brotherhood calls for its followers to demonstrate after Friday 's weekly prayers in Egypt , the first time in the current round of unrest that the largest opposition bloc has told supporters to take to the streets .
Protesters in Egypt use social media to organize and spread images of demonstrations, with a Facebook page for Friday's planned protests surpassing 80,000 followers.
Egyptians demonstrate in Cairo demanding the resignation of President Hosni Mubarak, with the army deployed to enforce a curfew amid a nationwide uprising.
Looters at the Cairo Museum damaged two statues of King Tutankhamun, broke 13 glass showcases, and damaged 70 other antiquities.
Saudi King Abdullah expressed support for Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak and condemned protesters in Egypt as "infiltrators" seeking to destabilize the country.

Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak visits an armed services operations center to follow up on the security situation amid unrest, as Egypt's military arrests 450 people in Cairo and the government shuts down Al Jazeera's Cairo bureau.
Protests continue in Egypt as demonstrators defy a curfew, with the military deployed in full force in Cairo and President Mubarak appointing new cabinet members.
Iranian Foreign Minister Ali Akbar Salehi praises Egypt's protests, with Iran's parliament speaker also expressing support for uprisings against dictatorial regimes.
Egyptian demonstrators demanding the resignation of President Mubarak carry the body of a dead protestor past army tanks.
Egyptian authorities shut down the offices of Al Jazeera amid the uprising in Egypt.

Massive protests in Egypt demanding the end of President Hosni Mubarak's 30-year rule have resulted in at least 38 deaths, with the Obama administration urging restraint and a process of national dialogue for political and economic reform.
Mohamed ElBaradei appeared in Cairo's Liberation Square during the sixth day of protests, telling the crowd that what they started can never be pushed back.

Egypt braces for a "march of millions" in anti-government protests as President Hosni Mubarak's government shuts down rail, mobile phone and internet services ahead of planned demonstrations calling for his ouster.
Untold thousands of Egyptians have ignored government curfews and clashed with police over demands that President Hosni Mubarak resign.
A record crowd of Egyptians gathered in Cairo's Tahrir Square for a "march of millions" demonstration demanding President Hosni Mubarak's departure.
President Hosni Mubarak announced he will not run for re-election in September, following eight days of growing demonstrations in Egypt.

Heavy gunfire erupted in central Cairo's Tahrir Square as supporters and opponents of Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak clashed, with the health ministry reporting three killed and 639 wounded in Wednesday's violence.
Journalists covering unrest in Egypt reported being beaten, arrested, and harassed by security forces and police, leading to sharply limited television coverage of the protests.

U.S. officials discuss ways to move Egypt's political transition forward and call for embattled Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak to leave office and for inclusive negotiations to begin immediately with his political opponents.

A Muslim Brotherhood spokesman says the organization will not participate in Egypt's general election planned for September and that talks on Egypt's future should occur only after President Hosni Mubarak steps down.
Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak refuses to step down immediately, saying he will remain until September despite ongoing anti-government protests demanding his departure.
The Mubarak regime shut down the internet in Egypt in a failed attempt to disrupt pro-democracy forces, catching human rights advocates and dissidents off guard.
Tens of thousands of protesters gather in Cairo's Tahrir Square for a "Day of Departure" rally demanding President Hosni Mubarak relinquish power, but Mubarak does not step down.

Egyptian troops move onto the streets to enforce a curfew as protesters battle police in Cairo, Suez and Alexandria demanding an end to President Hosni Mubarak's rule, and Mubarak announces he has fired his Cabinet and named Omar Suleiman as vice president.

President Obama condemns attacks on journalists in Egypt amid criticism that the assaults were orchestrated by President Hosni Mubarak to suppress international coverage of bloodshed by pro-government operatives against peaceful protesters.

Palestinians demonstrating in support of Egyptian anti-government protesters in Ramallah were forcibly disbanded when a few dozen men in plain clothes disrupted the protest, sparking fistfights that injured at least two people.
Egyptian television networks report that Google executive Wael Ghonim, missing since January 28 after a purported arrest in Cairo, is to be released Monday.
Protests in Egypt continue as demonstrators refuse to leave Cairo's Liberation Square until Hosni Mubarak steps down, while Mubarak also refuses to budge.

Wael Ghonim, a 30-year-old Egyptian internet activist, was released after 12 days in detention and gave an emotional television interview that energized popular Egyptian protests against President Hosni Mubarak.

Human Rights Watch issues a report alleging that numerous Arab governments, including the Palestinian Authority and Hamas, have used violence to quash demonstrations in the wake of mass protests in Egypt.
Thousands of Egyptian workers go on strike demanding better compensation and transparency in executive salaries as protests demanding President Hosni Mubarak's resignation enter their 17th day.
Mohamed ElBaradei warns that Egypt will explode and the army must save the country now after President Hosni Mubarak announces he will not step down before September elections.

Protests in Egypt continue on Day 17, with lawyers toppling barricades at Cairo's Abdeen Palace and petroleum, railway, and telecommunications employees striking in solidarity, as demonstrators are angered by President Hosni Mubarak's refusal to immediately step down.
Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak delegates powers to Vice President Omar Suleiman but remains titular head of the country, while Suleiman is described as the de facto president.
Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak stepped down and handed over power to the military after nearly three decades of rule, following popular protests that began January 25.
Yemen expresses confidence that Egypt's military council will steer the nation through its political crisis following Hosni Mubarak's ouster.
Egyptians celebrate in Tahrir Square the day after the revolution that brought down President Hosni Mubarak, while the military council maintains the existing government as a caretaker.
Egypt's military suspends the constitution and announces a transition government will run the country for six months or until parliamentary elections, following the ouster of President Hosni Mubarak.
